definition: In this context, misattribution means wrongly assigning causality to one’s conscious intention, so a person experiences their will as the cause of an action even though the actual causal processes are elsewhere. The packet specifically describes free will as a subjective experience built on this mistaken sense of authorship.

reasons: The packet supports misattribution as a misattribution of causality underlying the experience of free will, but it does not specifically support the added claim that causality is wrongly assigned to one’s conscious intention or that the ‘actual causal processes are elsewhere.’

‘Mistaken sense of authorship’ is not stated in the packet and goes beyond the source’s wording; the packet instead frames free will as an experiential phenomenon shaped by conditioning and causal determinism.
The definition is somewhat over-specific for the packet: it presents a particular causal explanation of conscious intention that is not directly supported as written.

The packet does not explicitly support the phrase that the “person experiences their will as the cause of an action” (it mentions misattribution of causality, but not this specific authorship/experienced-will-as-cause formulation).

The definition claims the packet “specifically describes free will as a subjective experience built on this mistaken sense of authorship”; the packet supports that free will is an illusory/experiential phenomenon based on subjective experience and misattribution of causality, but it does not mention “authorship” or a “sense of authorship.”
